grammar.title: Present Perfect

points: Use have with I, you, we, they; has with he, she, it.
Use it for experiences and for past actions whose result matters now.
Signal words: ever, never, already, yet, just, since, for, recently.
Example: The region has experienced three disasters in six weeks.

grammar.lead: Complete the sentences, then build your own with the present perfect.

grammar.title: Past Passive

points: Use the passive when the action matters more than who did it.
was with a singular subject, were with a plural subject.
Add by + agent only when it is useful: The town was destroyed by the flood.

grammar.lead: Complete the sentences with the past passive, then build them word by word.

grammar.title: Present Perfect or Past Simple?

rule.formula: Finished time → Past Simple (V2) · Up to now → Present Perfect (have/has + V3)
points: Past simple with a finished time: last August, in 2023, when she was young.
Present perfect with time up to now: since, for, so far, recently, yet.
Passive forms follow the same rule: was destroyed / has been destroyed.

grammar.lead: Look for the time words, then choose the tense.

examples.en: The river has flooded the town three times this year.
examples.note: Present perfect: this year is not finished, and the result matters now.

examples.en: The river flooded the town in 2023.
examples.note: Past simple: a finished time (2023). We are not connecting it to now.

l1Errors.wrong: I am live in Almaty since 2019.
l1Errors.right: I have lived in Almaty since 2019.
l1Errors.why: Russian and Kazakh often use a present-tense verb for a situation that started in the past and goes on. English needs the present perfect with since and for.

l1Errors.wrong: She has went to the shelter.
l1Errors.right: She has gone to the shelter.
l1Errors.why: After have or has, use the past participle (V3: gone), not the past simple form (V2: went).

notice.prompt: Tap every word that belongs to a present perfect verb (have or has plus the participle).
notice.text: Heavy rain has fallen on Marlowe for three days. The river has flooded two streets, but nobody has been hurt. In 2019 a similar flood destroyed the old bridge.
notice.explanation: Present perfect is has or have plus the past participle. "destroyed" is past simple because 2019 is a finished time.

complete.prompt: The mayor ___ (visit) the shelter twice this week.
complete.explanation: This week is not finished, so use the present perfect: has + visited.
Yet with a negative sentence needs the present perfect: have not + left (V3).

complete.prompt: Complete the question: ___ (you / ever / see) a flood?
complete.explanation: A question about experience: Have + subject + ever + V3 (seen).
Since a point in time, still true now: present perfect. My sister is she, so has.
Already goes between have and the participle, or at the end.

answers: The river has flooded two streets.
build.explanation: River is singular, so has; the verb after has is flooded (V3). Start with a capital letter and end with a full stop.

answers: Have you ever seen a tornado?
build.explanation: Question order: Have + subject + ever + V3. Seen is the participle; saw is past simple.

answers: We have not heard the news yet.
build.explanation: Have + not + V3, and yet goes at the end. We takes have, not has.

transform.prompt: Rewrite with the present perfect and already.
answers: The council has already repaired the roads.
The council has repaired the roads already.
transform.explanation: Present perfect: has + repaired. Already goes before the participle or at the end.

transform.prompt: Rewrite as a question with ever.
answers: Have you ever seen a volcano?
transform.explanation: Experience question: Have + you + ever + V3 (seen).

transform.prompt: Rewrite in the negative with yet.
answers: The workers have not finished the repairs yet.
The workers haven't finished the repairs yet.
transform.explanation: Negative present perfect: have not + V3, with yet at the end.

produce.prompt: Write 2 sentences about a storm, flood or other event you know about. Use the present perfect at least twice.
checklist: I used has or have before the verb.

readingHtml:
The Great Flood of Marlowe

Six weeks, three disasters: how one town has learned to live with extreme weather

A.In the spring of 2023, heavy rain fell on the town of Marlowe for three days. More than 200 millimetres of rain fell in the first two days alone. The river in the town centre was usually calm, but the rain was too much. The water level rose quickly. On the third day, the river overflowed. Water covered the streets and entered the ground floors of many houses. Marlowe was the town worst affected by the flood.

B.When the flood started, the local council told everyone to evacuate. The evacuation was organised by the fire service. Rescue teams used small boats to travel through the streets. They helped elderly people and children who were trapped in their homes. The water stayed in the town for a whole week.

C.After the water went down, the people of Marlowe began to clean up. The council provided free food and water. Now, the town is making a plan. They want to build new defences to protect the town from future floods.

D.Two weeks after the flood, a heat wave arrived. For ten consecutive days, temperatures rose above 42°C. The air was hot and humid, and nobody could sleep well. There was almost no rain, and the region was soon in a drought.

E.At the end of the heat wave, a wildfire started in the dry forest north of the town. More than 400 hectares of forest were destroyed. Firefighters worked for eleven days before the fire was put out. Several farms were damaged, but no lives were lost. Years of deforestation had already made the hills weak, and after the fire a small landslide blocked one road.

F.Marlowe has experienced three disasters in just six weeks. Since then, the council has created a new warning system, and from next summer cooling centres will open automatically when the temperature reaches 38°C. Scientists have warned that a warmer atmosphere makes heat waves and floods more likely. In one way, though, the town is lucky. It lies on a stable part of the Earth's crust, so even a small tremor is rare, and no earthquake with a magnitude above 3 has ever been recorded there. It is far from any volcano, so an eruption is impossible, and it is too far from the sea for a tsunami. Hurricanes and tornadoes have never reached the region, and with no mountains nearby, people in Marlowe have only seen blizzards and avalanches on the news.
